summary.case_overview: This judgment disposes of a batch of writ petitions filed under Article 32 of the Constitution of India challenging the constitutional validity of several provisions regulating online speech and content [Page 18] [Page 20]. The Supreme Court of India examined the validity of Section 66A, Section 69A, and Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, along with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009, the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules, 2011, and Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act, 1960 [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 18] [Page 20] [Page 102]. The Court declared Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act unconstitutional as they violated Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution and were not saved by Article 19(2) [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 8] [Page 14] [Page 112]. The Court upheld Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules [Page 1] [Page 14] [Page 112], and upheld Section 79 of the IT Act and Rule 3(4) of the 2011 Intermediary Guidelines Rules subject to reading them down to require actual knowledge via a court order or government notification [Page 2] [Page 15] [Page 16] [Page 112].
summary.facts_of_case: Section 66A was inserted into the Information Technology Act, 2000 by an Amendment Act of 2009 with effect from October 27, 2009, penalizing the sending of offensive, false, or annoying messages through a computer resource or communication device [Page 20]. Multiple writ petitions were filed under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging Section 66A after instances of its application against individuals using the internet [Page 18] [Page 20]. Petitioners also challenged related legal provisions, including Section 69A of the IT Act providing for blocking public access to information [Page 21] [Page 106], Section 79 of the IT Act regarding intermediary liability exemptions [Page 107] [Page 109], the associated 2009 Blocking Rules and 2011 Intermediary Guidelines Rules [Page 106] [Page 110], and Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act penalizing causing annoyance in an indecent manner [Page 102].
summary.legal_issues:
1. Whether Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is constitutionally invalid for violating Article 19(1)(a) and not being saved under Article 19(2) of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 8] [Page 20] [Page 35].
2. Whether Section 66A is constitutionally invalid under Article 14 of the Constitution on the ground of discrimination between internet communications and other mediums [Page 1] [Page 24] [Page 98].
3. Whether Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act falls outside the state legislature's legislative competence and violates Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution [Page 2] [Page 14] [Page 103] [Page 106].
4. Whether Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the 2009 Blocking Rules are constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 14] [Page 106] [Page 108].
5. Whether Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and Rule 3(4) of the 2011 Intermediary Guidelines Rules are constitutionally valid or require being read down [Page 2] [Page 15] [Page 16] [Page 110] [Page 111].
summary.important_arguments_or_content:
Petitioners' Arguments:
- Petitioners submitted that Section 66A casts an excessively wide net over all information on the internet, directly affecting the public's right to know and generating a chilling effect on free speech [Page 4] [Page 11] [Page 23] [Page 24].
- They argued that Section 66A lacks any proximate connection to the eight subject matters permitted under Article 19(2) [Page 8] [Page 35].
- They contended that expressions in Section 66A are vague, open-ended, and undefined, failing to define guilt or provide clear guidance [Page 1] [Page 8] [Page 10] [Page 61].
- Petitioners argued that Section 66A violates Article 14 because there is no intelligible differentia between users of the internet and users of other communication mediums [Page 24] [Page 98].
- Regarding Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act, petitioners contended that the State Legislature lacked legislative competence and that the section was impermissibly vague [Page 103] [Page 104] [Page 106].
- On Section 69A and the 2009 Rules, petitioners argued that no pre-decisional hearing was provided to the originator of information and confidentiality provisions affected fundamental rights [Page 108].
- On Section 79 and the 2011 Rules, petitioners submitted that intermediaries were improperly required to exercise their own judgment to disable content upon receiving notice [Page 110].

Respondents' Arguments:
- The Additional Solicitor General defended Section 66A, arguing there is a presumption of constitutionality and that the legislature understands the needs of the people [Page 24].
- He argued that loose language was deployed to combat novel methods of disturbing rights over the internet and that vagueness is not a ground to invalidate a statute if it is legislatively competent [Page 24].
- He submitted that the possibility of abuse cannot render a statute invalid and provided an assurance that the provision would be administered reasonably [Page 24] [Page 93].
- He argued that internet speech differs significantly from print or broadcast media because content travels like lightning to millions globally [Page 41] [Page 60] [Page 98].
- He maintained that Section 118 of the Kerala Police Act fell within List II Entry 2 or List III Entry 1 [Page 103] [Page 105].
summary.court_reasoning:
1. Section 66A and Article 19(1)(a): Freedom of speech encompasses discussion, advocacy, and incitement; speech can only be restricted under Article 19(2) when discussion or advocacy reaches the level of incitement [Page 3] [Page 29]. Section 66A makes no distinction between discussion/advocacy and incitement and has no proximate relationship to public order, defamation, incitement to an offence, or decency/morality [Page 4] [Page 6] [Page 7] [Page 8]. The section lacks mens rea ingredients and uses completely open-ended and vague terms, causing a chilling effect on free speech and suffering from overbreadth [Page 8] [Page 9] [Page 10] [Page 11].
2. Doctrine of Severability & Abuse: Section 66A cannot be saved by assurances of reasonable administration because an invalid statute cannot be validated by proper administration [Page 12] [Page 94]. No part of Section 66A is severable because its language covers restrictions both within and outside constitutionally permissible limits [Page 12] [Page 95] [Page 97].
3. Section 66A and Article 14: Internet speech provides a unique platform requiring little or no payment to air views globally and instantly; there is an intelligible differentia between internet speech and other mediums of communication, so the Article 14 challenge fails [Page 1] [Page 13] [Page 98] [Page 99].
4. Section 118(d) of Kerala Police Act: The Kerala Police Act in pith and substance falls within Entry 2 List II and Entry 1 List III, establishing legislative competence [Page 14] [Page 104] [Page 105]. However, Section 118(d) suffers from the same vagueness and overbreadth as Section 66A and is unconstitutional under Article 19(1)(a) [Page 14] [Page 106].
5. Section 69A and 2009 Rules: Section 69A is a narrowly drawn provision with adequate procedural safeguards (written reasoned orders, relatable to Article 19(2), review committee, hearing to originators/intermediaries), making it and the 2009 Rules valid [Page 14] [Page 15] [Page 106] [Page 108].
6. Section 79 and 2011 Rules: Section 79 is an exemption provision. To prevent intermediaries from having to judge millions of content removal requests, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(4) of the 2011 Rules are read down to mean that actual knowledge must be received through a court order or notification by the appropriate government or its agency strictly conforming to Article 19(2) subjects [Page 15] [Page 16] [Page 111] [Page 112].
summary.decision_or_conclusion:
The Supreme Court concluded and ordered that:
1. Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is struck down in its entirety as violative of Article 19(1)(a) and not saved under Article 19(2) [Page 1] [Page 8] [Page 112].
2. Section 69A of the IT Act and the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 are constitutionally valid [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 112].
3. Section 79 of the IT Act is valid, subject to Section 79(3)(b) being read down to mean that an intermediary must receive actual knowledge from a court order or notification by the appropriate government/agency regarding unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) [Page 2] [Page 16] [Page 112].
4. The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules, 2011 are valid, subject to Rule 3(4) being read down in the same manner as Section 79(3)(b) [Page 2] [Page 16] [Page 112].
5. Section 118(d) of the Kerala Police Act is struck down as violative of Article 19(1)(a) and not saved under Article 19(2) [Page 2] [Page 14] [Page 112].
6. All writ petitions were disposed of in these terms [Page 3] [Page 112].
